say: Good morning, Data Detectives! A graph is a picture of numbers. A good detective reads it carefully, and also checks whether the picture is telling the truth.
Today we read line graphs and tables, find numbers that are missing, and catch a graph that tries to trick us. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
Here are four tiny graphs with no numbers at all. I will read a story. Point to the graph that tells the story, and be ready to say why.
Listen: a bath filling up with water. Which line? Why not the one that goes up and then down?
You will plot the queue at a chicken rice stall from 11:00 to 2:00. Before you plot: at what time do you think the queue is longest? Write your guess at the top of your grid.
stuck: Stuck on the scale: the biggest number is 22. If each line is 2 people, how many lines do you need to reach 22?
Points in the wrong place: put your finger on the time, go straight up, then check the number on the side.
Finished early: between which two times did the queue grow the most? Show it on your graph without working out every change.

say: “First the title and the axes: books borrowed, Monday to Friday. Then the scale: each line on the side is worth 10. Tuesday’s point is on the 40 line, so 40. Monday’s point is halfway between 20 and 30, so 25.”

“Which day had the biggest change? I list each change: Monday to Tuesday up 15, Tuesday to Wednesday down 5, Wednesday to Thursday up 25, Thursday to Friday down 10. The biggest increase is 25, and on the graph it is the steepest line going up.”
“A table with missing numbers: Ali’s row must add up to 61. 61 − 26 = 35. I fill the rows first, then the columns. Last, I check: the column totals and the row totals must give the same grand total.”

do: Point to a line and ask: “Is this an increase or a decrease? By how much?”
Ask: “What is each line on the side worth? How do you know?”
Ask: “How can you check your missing number?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find what one line on the scale is worth before you read anything.”
Hint 2: “Write the change between each pair of neighbours, with up or down.”
Hint 3: “Add the numbers you know, then take them away from the total.”

say: “Two graphs show the same numbers, but one line looks much steeper. How can that be?”
ask: “Two graphs show the same numbers, but one line looks much steeper. How can that be?”
The scales are different. If a scale starts at a big number, or each line is worth very little, a small change looks huge.

say: “Today you read graphs like detectives: scale first, then the changes, and you caught a graph that was trying to trick you.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p4l9-title.note: Objective: Read values and trends from line graphs (using the scale), find the biggest increase or decrease, find missing values in tables and graphs from totals and patterns, compare two lines on one graph, and explain why a graph with a different scale can mislead. Thinking strategies today: READ THE SCALE FIRST, LIST THE CHANGES, and WORK FROM THE TOTAL. Materials: Mini whiteboards, a ruler and two coloured pencils per child, printed blank graph grids (or squared paper), the queue table for the explore task. Online: children use a printed blank grid or squared paper and check it against the graphs the tutor plots on the slides; while children call out where each point goes (nothing is held up to the camera). Time plan (90 minutes in all; every part has a budget and there is a 2-minute standing buffer inside the page-2 block). Opening 0 to 1.5. Sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 6.5 (puzzle 1 about 60 seconds, puzzle 2 about 90 seconds, then ONE check moment for both puzzles; answers ticked or said together on three; nothing held up to the camera, nobody marked). Warm-up game 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds), quick questions 8.5 to 11.5 (three questions). Explore 11.5 to 26 (the only breakout of the first half: about 60 seconds each way, closed by a 60-second timer; a Go further what-if is on the slide from the start; two debrief questions). Teaching 26 to 32.5 (click to reveal each step and answer; the one "your turn" slide is optional: skip it if you are behind). Brain break 32.5 to 36 (water and toilet first, then the game; clock check at the end of the break: if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item, never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back). Worksheet 36 to 80: page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 36 to 54, check together 54 to 56, short teaching before page 2 56 to 60, page 2 on your own 60 to 77.5 (the last 2 minutes are the standing buffer: if earlier parts ran long, spend the buffer first, then the choice questions, and never the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back), check together 77.5 to 80. Talk time 80 to 84.5 (one minute of pair talk, no breakout; one minute is the tool question: where did you use today's tool?). Exit ticket 84.5 to 87.5. Looking back 87.5 to 90 (common look-back: 90-second timer, then about 60 seconds to stamp journals). This page ends at question 2. After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children). SPINE: Today's tool is Make a table. Make a table, fill it row by row and look down the columns. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p4l9-check.note: Minutes 1.5 to 6.5 (5 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. Give about 60 seconds for puzzle 1 and about 90 seconds for puzzle 2. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and said together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Make ONE check for both puzzles, after puzzle 2: children say the answers together on three. Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards or paper held up in front of the group or to the camera, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) Tuesday sold the most (45). Wednesday sold the fewest (25). 2) 125. Halfway between 100 and 150 is 100 + 25. A GOOD REASON: Read the scale first: what is each line worth? Halfway between two lines is half of the step. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. ON PAGE 1 (printed): "This page ends at question 2. After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l9-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 8.5 (one short round, about 90 seconds: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Which graph tells the story? The graphs have no numbers on purpose: we read the SHAPE. Read story 1 aloud. Children point at (or write the letter of) the matching graph, then say why before you click. Clicks reveal the answers in order. Answers: 1) Graph C: the water goes up steadily. 2) Graph A: people arrive for lunch, then leave. 3) Graph D: the candle gets shorter steadily. 4) Graph B: nothing changes, so the line is flat. Listen for "steep" and "flat": we use those words all lesson.

p4l9-warm2.note: Minutes 8.5 to 11.5. Three questions, about 30 seconds each: write it, say the answer together on three, then click. No follow-up questions. Each one is a skill for today: 1) 27, the size of a change. 2) 45, reading halfway between two grid lines. 3) 100: add 85 + 15. The other two warm-up questions (four numbers total 200; which is the bigger change, 120 to 95 or 60 to 90) are in the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math.

p4l9-explore1.note: Minutes 11.5 to 22.5. Pairs plot the queue on a blank grid (online: printed grid or squared paper on camera). Ask them to predict first: when is the queue longest? Let pairs choose their own scale: lines worth 1, 2 or 5 all work if the lines are equal steps; a scale of 1 needs 22 lines. Hint for anyone unsure: try 2 per line (the biggest number is 22, so 12 lines are enough). Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: between which two times did the queue grow the most? Can you see it without working out every change? GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of the explore, so nobody waits): Draw the same graph again with a different scale. Does the story look different? Why? Answer: Yes. A scale with small steps, or one that starts above 0, makes the line look steeper; big steps make it look flatter. The numbers are the same: only the picture changed.

p4l9-explore2.note: Minutes 22.5 to 26. Pencils down (or when the 60-second timer closes the rooms), then gather pairs and compare graphs. Two debrief questions only: are the shapes the same even if the scales are different? (Yes, if the steps are equal.) Answers: 1) 12:30, with 22 people. 2) 11:30 to 12:00: up 9 (the steepest line going up; the changes are up 5, up 9, up 4, down 7, down 8, down 4). The third question (the best time to buy chicken rice: 2:00 with 3 people, or 11:00 with 4) is not asked. Do NOT teach the steepest-line idea yet if nobody notices it: the next slides teach it.

p4l9-teach1.note: Teach. Click through the steps, then the red and teal reading lines. Think-aloud: "First the title and the axes, so I know what is counted and when. Then the scale: 0, 10, 20 on the numbered lines, so each numbered line is worth 10, and the faint line between is 5. Tuesday's point sits on the 40 line. Monday's point is halfway between 20 and 30: 25." Ask children to read Wednesday (35), Thursday (60) and Friday (50) on whiteboards. Common mistake: reading each line as 1.

p4l9-we1.note: Click to list each change, then the highlight, the answer and the rule. Think-aloud: "I list the change between each pair of neighbours and write up or down. The biggest increase is 25, Wednesday to Thursday. Look: on the graph it is the steepest line going up. So I can spot the biggest change by looking, then check it by working out." Ask: "Which is the biggest DEcrease?" (Thursday to Friday, 10). Worksheet Q1 asks for both.

p4l9-we2.note: Click: each step, then its row fills in. Think-aloud: "A row must add up to its total. Ali has 26 and a missing number, total 61: 61 − 26 = 35. Then Mei. Ravi's total is the two numbers added. Last, I add down the columns. Then the best part: the check. The column totals and the row totals must both make the same grand total, 178. If they do not, I have made a mistake somewhere." Worksheet Q2 is the same kind of table.

p4l9-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 30 + 45 + 35 = 110, 150 − 110 = 40. b) 60 − 28 = 32. c) 90 shared equally: 45 and 45. Check each by adding back up to the total.

p4l9-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Reading the scale as 1 for each line when each line is worth 10 (or 5), so 75 is read as 7 and a half. (2) Looking only for the biggest increase and missing a bigger decrease, or comparing the heights of points instead of the change between them. (3) Comparing two graphs by how steep the lines look without checking where each scale starts and what each line is worth.

p4l9-break.note: 3.5 minutes: water and toilet FIRST (about one minute), then the game (about two minutes), then back in your seats. CLOCK CHECK at the end of the break (minute 36): if you are more than 1.5 minutes behind, skip the next optional item (the "your turn" slide, a second speaker-note question), never a check, the exit ticket or Looking back. Stories to call: a slow climb then flat; a fast drop; up, up, up then a crash; flat, then a sudden jump. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p4l9-ws1.note: Minutes 36 to 54. Page 1 ends at Q2. Walk around. Ask "What is one line worth?" and "How can you check?" before giving any help. Q1d asks for a reason from the story: the stall is next to an office. CHOOSING (printed on page 1: "This page ends at question 2. After question 2 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder."): invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l9-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains. Q1: the changes are up 15, down 5, up 25, down 10, down 40, up 5. Saturday and Sunday: 25 + 30 = 55. Q2: 85 − 38 = 47, 70 − 29 = 41, 45 + 52 = 97; check 124 + 128 = 252 = 85 + 70 + 97. b) Week 3 is 6 more for each of the 3 classes: 128 + 18 = 146.

p4l9-teachtwo.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 has two lines). Use the key (legend) first: "Which line is which?" Click the steps. Think-aloud: "Q starts taller, but P grows faster: its line is steeper. Every week P catches up by 2 cm. The gap was 6, then 4, then 2, then 0: they cross at week 4. After that P is taller." Your turn: 20 − 18 = 2 cm. Do not do Q3 for them: Ali and Mei have different numbers.

p4l9-teachsteps.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4, Siti's pages). Ask first: "How many jumps from Day 1 to Day 4?" Many children say 4. Count the gaps on the graph: 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4: 3 jumps. Click the steps, then the full line appears. Check: 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 all go up by 4. Total: 8 + 12 + 16 + 20 + 24 = 80 (or 5 days × the middle day, 16).

p4l9-teachscale.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5, the two shops). Ask first: "Which car park got much busier?" Most children say Graph 2. Then let them read the numbers from both graphs: they are the same! Click. Think-aloud: "Graph 2 does not start at 0. It starts at 50, and each line is only 2, so a small change looks huge. Graph 1 starts at 0, so the same change looks tiny. Neither graph is wrong, but Graph 2 can trick you." Someone who wants the change to look big, like an advert, would draw Graph 2.

p4l9-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who still reads every line as 1, and who compares the graphs by their look only. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q3 and Q4 first. Q5 is a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which. BUFFER: the last 2 minutes of this block (minute 75.5 to 77.5) are the standing buffer. If earlier parts ran long, page 2 starts late and the buffer is spent first, then the choice questions at the end of the page. Never shorten the checks, the exit ticket or Looking back. Say nothing about the buffer to the children.

p4l9-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3: Ali goes up $10 a week, Mei $5; the gap of $20 in week 1 closes by $5 each week, so they meet in week 5 ($50) and Ali is ahead from week 6. Week 8: Ali 80, Mei 65. Q4: Day 2 to Day 5 is 3 jumps, 26 − 14 = 12, 12 ÷ 3 = 4; total 10 + 14 + 18 + 22 + 26 = 90. Q5: A goes 20 to 80, B goes 44 to 56. The lines look the same because each graph was stretched to fit its own scale.

p4l9-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) Neither: both have 34 girls. (4A: 28 + 6 = 34. 4B: 63 − 5 = 58, 58 ÷ 2 = 29 boys, 29 + 5 = 34 girls.) 2) Ali 175 and Mei 275, so Mei has 100 more. She is not right: double Ali's is 350, and 275 is less than that. (Her point is more than twice as many lines up, 7 against 3, but the scale starts at 100, so counting lines gives the wrong picture.) 3) Monday 40, Tuesday 55, Wednesday 70, Thursday 55, Friday 40. Friday: 40 cups. Thursday (55) matches Tuesday (55). 4) From age 7 to 8 (7 cm). Altogether 17 cm.

p4l9-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q6. Answers: 1) A 34, B 17, C 27, D 22. 2) After 4 hours: 56 litres each.

p4l9-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: In Q1, how many equal bars can you see if you take away the 10 and the 22? In Q2, what happens to the GAP between the tanks every hour? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l9-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the bar model turns "twice as many" and "10 more" into equal bars; check 34 + 17 + 27 + 22 = 100. Q2: a table works (keep going hour by hour), but the gap idea is quicker: Tank A goes down and Tank B goes up, so the gap shrinks by both amounts each hour. On a line graph the two lines cross at hour 4, at 56 litres. After that, Tank B has more.

p4l9-gap-spin.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it while some pairs are working or have finished, or use it live as an extra warm-up or tutor-bank question; never at a fixed minute, and it never takes time from the plan. ADDED ITEM spin (a slide-only addition for the skill gap "Spinners with unequal parts"; it is not in the printed workbook). TOOL: Draw it. SAY: The picture is a fair way to see the parts of one whole circle. Think of the whole as 6 equal slices. ASK: How many slices is yellow? Green? How many are left for blue? LISTEN FOR: Common denominator 6: 3/6, 2/6, 1/6. Listen for "more of the circle means more likely". For (c) accept "about", never "exactly". Everyone writes the answer on their own paper, then say the answer together on three, then click the answer box. Nobody holds anything up, nobody is marked, and passing is always fine. ANSWER: (a) 1/6. (b) Yellow. (c) About 30 times (green about 20, blue about 10). WHY: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6, so blue is 1/6. Yellow has the biggest part. 1/2 of 60 = 30, 1/3 of 60 = 20, 1/6 of 60 = 10.

p4l9-talk.note: Minutes 80 to 84.5. Pair talk is 1 minute (no breakout rooms: children tell the grown-up beside them, or write one sentence), then share. Answer: the scales are different. If a scale starts at a big number, or each line is worth very little, a small change looks huge. Not asked in class (moved to the Weekly Dose of Thinking Math): "How would you draw a fair graph if you wanted to compare two shops?" (use the same scale for both graphs, starting at 0). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake. TOOL MINUTE: Talk time is one minute longer than before (the common look-back is shorter). Spend it on the question on the slide: where did you use today's tool, and what did it help you see? Listen for the tool named, not for the answer; a child may pass.

p4l9-exit.note: Minutes 84.5 to 87.5. Answer: Tuesday to Wednesday, a decrease of 30 (the other changes are up 15 and up 25). Watch for children who choose Wednesday to Thursday (the biggest INCREASE, 25). Extension: draw two line graphs of 52, 54, 56, 58, one that makes the change look huge and one that makes it look tiny.

p4l9-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 87.5 to 90. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals.
